item.title: When Communication Gets Tough With Hearing Loss, Just Breathe
item.description:
Stress

When Communication Gets Tough With Hearing Loss, Just Breathe

Have hearing loss? Mindful breathing can ease the stress of tough conversations.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Three slow, mindful breaths can shift the body from fight-or-flight into a calmer, rest-and-digest state.
  • Hearing loss creates ongoing communication stress, which can undermine effective self-advocacy.
  • Pausing to breathe before reacting helps you move from frustration to problem-solving.

Sweating in the hot yoga room, I work to hold the posture. I fall out, but try again. And again. It's a difficult practice, so struggle is normal and expected. The teacher reminds us to focus on our breath. While we can't control the heat or how long she holds the postures, we can control our response, helping us stay calm and focused amid the challenge.

Despite my discomfort, I try to breathe in and out slowly—four to six counts for my inhale, and four to six counts for my exhale. I call it my yoga breathing, and it helps me deal with stressful situations both on and off my mat—including the frustrations of living with hearing loss.

Source: Alexey Demidov / Unsplash

What Is Yoga Breathing?

When practicing yoga, the goal is to breathe in and out through the nose, keeping the length and depth of the inhale and exhale balanced. For example, if you breathe in for four counts, you breathe out for four counts. Keeping your mouth closed signals the body that all is well, allowing the nervous system to relax and bringing a feeling of calm.

Why Does Mindful Breathing Help Us Relax?

The human autonomic nervous system has two main parts: the sympathetic nervous system, which controls the body's response to a perceived threat or stressor (fight or flight), and the parasympathetic nervous system, which controls homeostasis (rest and digest). In fight or flight, breathing becomes shallow and rapid to increase oxygen flow, making our bodies ready for action. In rest and digest, the opposite happens—breathing deepens and slows, returning the body to calm.

These responses are automatic, but you can trigger them through mindful breathing. Three slow, mindful breaths are all it takes to elicit rest and digest, lowering our blood pressure and our heart rate. It's like a switch telling the body it can relax because all is well.

Mindful Breathing and Hearing Loss

Hearing loss is stressful.

Will I be able to enjoy this dinner with friends if they forget to speak one at a time?

How will I understand the doctor’s instructions from behind a mask?

What if this Zoom meeting doesn’t have captions?

Simply participating in a conversation with hearing loss can be exhausting, especially a difficult one. It's like playing a game of Wheel of Fortune where some of the letters are filled in, and others are missing. We use speechreading and other strategies to help fill in these blanks so we can understand what people are saying. But then, of course, we aren't finished, because now we need to reply. It takes a lot of mental energy and doesn't always go perfectly, creating stress, frustration, and even anger.

article continues after advertisement

But negative emotions won't solve communication problems. In fact, stress can elicit fight or flight—the exact opposite of the calm self-advocacy mindset we need to communicate well. Mindful breathing can help.

When I face a particularly frustrating listening experience, rather than panic or give up, I try to just breathe. With three mindful breaths, I calm my heart rate and switch my body to a more restful state. Then I can more easily shift my focus from worrying about what I can't hear to taking the steps I need to communicate better.

H.E.A.R. Your Way to Better Conversations

One tool I rely on is H.E.A.R., which we introduce in Hear & Beyond: Live Skillfully With Hearing Loss. H.E.A.R. helps you assess any listening situation, evaluate possible solutions, and advocate for your needs:

  • H — Hearing check: Assess the listening situation. Can you hear the person you are talking to? If not, changes are needed.
  • E — Evaluate: Consider what solutions might help, given the specific challenges you've identified. Some may be environmental (switching to a different seat) while others may involve communication partners (asking them to speak louder or slower).
  • A — Articulate: Let your communication partners know what would help you understand them better so you can participate. Hearing loss is invisible, so if you don't articulate your needs, change is unlikely.
  • R — Revise and Remind: If the environment or your listening partners change, repeat the steps. Sometimes, gentle reminders are needed even within a conversation if our communication partners slip back into old speaking patterns.

Just Breathe...

But perhaps the real first step is just to breathe.

Back in the yoga room, when I fall out of a pose for the third time, I don't panic. I breathe—and I try again. The next time a conversation overwhelms you, try the same thing: three slow breaths before you respond.

Copyright: Shari Eberts. A version of this post also appears on LivingWithHearingLoss.com.

item.title: What Is Pornmaxxing? "Love Island" and the Performance of Desire
item.description:
Pornography

What Is Pornmaxxing? "Love Island" and the Performance of Desire

Repeated exposure to hyper-sexual scripts desensitizes; the fallout is hardest on women.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • A generation is learning to perform desire and re-enact porn scripts, and the costs are serious.
  • The scripts are learned early and reinforced constantly, not just from pornography itself.
  • Platforms like "Love Island" gamify the porn scripts and reward performed desire with votes, fame, and prizes.

This post was co-written by Stephanie Boye and Cheralyn Leeby.

Joy, 19, is having sex with a boy who has his hands around her throat, calibrating her performance, moaning louder than the pressure warrants so he won't press harder. "I know they want to see me struggling to breathe," she says.

She is not enduring this. She is optimizing it for his pleasure, not her own.

There is a word for this; we call it pornmaxxing. Pornmaxxing borrows from looksmaxxing, the online practice of optimizing appearance to maximize perceived attractiveness. With pornmaxxing, young women suppress their own desires, dress the part, and perform pornified sexual behaviors to earn male attention. As one young woman said, "You have to be the porn star to get the guy."

The Shift No One Is Talking About

Typically, boys are the focus of any alarm about pornography and the aggression they might replicate. That worry is warranted. But it has crowded out a parallel story we have heard for more than a decade from young women.

A generation ago, women were devastated to discover their partners watched pornography. Pornmaxxing represents a profound inversion of that moment: the shift from resenting the porn actress to aspiring to become her.

The Scripts Get Absorbed Early

Anne was 9 years old when she first found pornography. "It was like a dictionary," she said. "I was trying to understand what sex was." By 15, she was reenacting scenes she watched with her boyfriend. Eventually, her searches escalated into more extreme content, and she disclosed that even though her “brain was disgusted, [her] body was aroused."

According to sexual script theory, sexual behavior is not instinctive, but learned (Gagnon & Simon, 1973). The scripts young people absorb provide instruction on how to interpret and act in sexual situations, and research confirms they exert particular influence on adolescents (Ward et al., 2022). Porn scripts consistently feature dominant males and accommodating and seductive females, with toned or fetishized bodies.

Young people who are not watching pornography are not insulated. The pornography-inspired scripts are everywhere in culture. Streaming shows, social media, and movies fill the gap. Research validates that diverse TV genres, from reality dating shows to dramas, shape teen sexual expectations (Ward et al., 2022). This includes who initiates, who submits, and what desire is supposed to look like. As always, sex sells, but today, innuendo is replaced with the explicit. The bedroom door is wide open.

article continues after advertisement

"Love Island" Is the Lab

"Love Island," in its eighth U.S. season on Peacock, is ranked as the number 1 original streaming series in the United States. On its surface, the show is a competition about love. In practice, it is an extended audition for desirability, or pornmaxxing.

"Love Island" does what pornography alone cannot. It makes the scripts socially acceptable and even entertaining. In real life, kissing multiple partners blindfolded and simulating sex acts for the approval of a crowd would be shocking. Yet on "Love Island," it rewards contestants, and recurring challenges gamify the porn scripts. With the “Heart Rate Challenge,” female contestants perform striptease routines while biometric monitors measure male arousal. The “Bad Boss” challenge asked the women to crawl upon a desk, gyrate, and seduce their “office crush.” The women who perform desirability flawlessly, emotionally uncomplicated, and relentlessly get to stay in the villa. "Love Island" incentivizes pornmaxxing behaviors through “votes,” follower counts, and prize money.

The Dosage Problem

There is something else at play: the dosage problem.

A generation ago, a teenager might encounter a sexualized image of a woman once a month, when the Victoria's Secret catalogue arrived. With "Love Island," a young person absorbs perfected, ranked, and highly sexualized bodies and behaviors for 90 minutes, five or six nights per week, almost all summer. Show the brain something often enough, and it stops reading it as shocking and starts seeing it as normal. This illustrates Wolpe's (1969) theory of systematic desensitization, where repeated exposure to a stimulus that is initially alarming becomes familiar, and with "Love Island," even expected.

The Costs Are Asymmetric

The goal is not to villainize the boys. Men are also re-enacting the scripts they consume. The boy with his hands on Joy's throat is running a script he didn’t write, conditioning him to pair dominance and sexual choking with pleasure. Pornmaxxing hits women hardest, but anyone can feel unworthy when they don’t measure up or empty after performing an idealized version of themselves. The lack of authenticity can undermine and obscure genuine connection.

While pornmaxxing is not gender specific, there are costs particular to women.

Jayne, 18, created an OnlyFans account at the request of a boy she had unrequited feelings for. "I didn't stop to ask whether any of this was what I actually wanted, but I liked the idea of him seeing me as hot," she said. The boy owned the account and the money earned. He pushed Jayne to do more, knowing that more graphic content earned more dollars. Jayne's story shows how pornmaxxing can cross the line and meet the legal definition of sex trafficking. She was willing to commercialize herself and sacrifice her self-worth to please a guy.

article continues after advertisement

Jayne, Joy, and Anne know exactly what pornmaxxing looks like from cultural saturation. However, Jayne deserves to be valued rather than objectified and monetized on OnlyFans. Anne deserves to feel and explore her organic desires. And Joy, like all young women, should never have to calibrate her performance to keep her partner from tightening his grip on her throat.

If we are to change this enculturated phenomenon, we need to name it and call it out and refuse to treat it as “normal.” Pornmaxxing gives us a word for what is happening, and that word belongs in conversations with parents and kids, partners, and peer groups, before it unconsciously shapes behavior. Critical thinking gives young people a pause between absorbing a pornographic script and choosing whether to act it out, publicly or privately. That pause is where media literacy starts, so that individuals can consciously create non-performative, real love, interest, and connection, not "Love Island."

item.title: Ear Ringing and the Residual Self
item.description:
Default Mode Network

Ear Ringing and the Residual Self

The Default Mode Network, tinnitus, and neuropsychology.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Brain imaging shows that chronic tinnitus involves networks far beyond just the auditory cortex.
  • Some of the strongest tinnitus-related brain changes occur in regions of the default mode network.
  • The default mode network helps construct self-awareness, identity, and autobiographical narrative.
  • Neuropsychological therapies may help reshape how the brain integrates tinnitus into the self.

A patient sits across from me and says: "I hear a loud ringing sound."

Two years later, the same patient says: "I'm a tinnitus sufferer."

The condition may be no different, but the brain's relationship to it has changed. What began as a perception has become part of a person's identity. Brain imaging suggests this transformation involves networks far beyond the auditory cortex, reshaping our understanding of chronic tinnitus and how it should be treated.

The Brain That Builds a Self

To understand what goes wrong in chronic tinnitus, it helps to understand what the brain is doing when it has downtime.

When you're not focused on a task — not reading, not driving, not solving a problem — your brain doesn't go quiet. It activates a network of regions devoted to inner narrative: reviewing memories, imagining futures, and evaluating yourself.

The part of our brain that does this is called the default mode network (DMN). It's the neural home of the self, the system that asks: Who am I, what has happened to me, and what does it mean?

What makes this relevant to tinnitus is where the strongest brain abnormalities in chronic tinnitus patients actually appear. It's not in the auditory cortex, as most people would expect. The most consistent findings across neuroimaging studies localize to the posterior cingulate cortex and the precuneus — two regions that sit at the center of autobiographical memory, self-reference, and narrative identity [1]. They are self regions, not hearing ones.

The Decision the Brain Makes

When tinnitus first appears, the brain asks a rapid series of questions: Is this important? Is it a threat? In most cases, the brain files it as unimportant and moves on. In general, when the brain sees a repeated signal of the same kind, it tends to block it using a process called sensory gating.

But in chronic tinnitus, the phantom sensation gets locked.

Research suggests the posterior cingulate cortex functions something like an acceptance switch. When it registers a signal as persistent and significant, the DMN begins integrating it — not as background noise, but as a fact about the person experiencing it. And as that integration deepens over time, the brain's network topology measurably reorganizes around the sound [2]. The sound stops being an event. It starts being a feature of the self.

This is why tinnitus loudness correlates so poorly with suffering. Patients with relatively quiet tinnitus by objective measures are profoundly disabled by it, while patients with loud tinnitus have found a way to live well. The audiogram doesn't predict distress. What predicts distress is, in part, how much of the self has reorganized around the sound. Add factors such as central sensitization, which amplify tinnitus perception, and the problem becomes even more pronounced.

article continues after advertisement

How Do You Treat the Default Mode Network?

Medication can reduce anxiety. It can dampen arousal, lift depression, quiet the nervous system's alarm signals. But medication cannot teach the brain a new relationship to experience. It cannot instruct the self-referential network to reconsider what it has filed under you.

That is precisely what certain neuropsychological interventions do.

  • Mindfulness works by introducing a wedge between sensation and self. The practice trains attention to observe experience without immediately incorporating it. Brain imaging shows that mindfulness measurably alters connectivity in the self-referential network — strengthening the brain's capacity to watch the default mode rather than be governed by it [3]. For tinnitus patients, this means the sound can be present without being central.
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) targets the narrative layer. The ringing itself may be unchangeable, but the story built around it — this is permanent, this is ruining everything, this defines my future — is not a fact. It is an interpretation. CBT works by surfacing that interpretation, testing it against evidence, and gradually replacing it with something more accurate and more livable. Neuroimaging studies show that CBT uniquely reduces the brain's tendency to default to self-referential rumination in ways that medication does not replicate [4].
  • Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) approaches the problem somewhat differently. Through acceptance, cognitive defusion, and committed action, ACT helps patients experience tinnitus without organizing their lives around it. The goal is to loosen the fusion between tinnitus and the self, allowing the sound to be present without defining who a person is.

All three approaches are intervening in the process by which the brain decides the sound belongs to the self. They are not treating the ear; they are treating the brain's story maker.

Why Multimodal Care Is Optimal Care

Psychological interventions that reshape the default mode network are powerful, but they cannot fully take hold when the brain is still experiencing significant fluctuations in symptoms. Medical stabilization must come first.

This is the model we follow at our tinnitus clinic. Medical stabilization and psychological rehabilitation run on parallel tracks because each makes the other more effective. One track reduces the signal; the other changes the relationship to it.

At its best, tinnitus care addresses the sound, the brain, and the self, not separately, but simultaneously.

item.title: What Not to Say to Someone With Chronic Pain
item.description:
Chronic Pain

What Not to Say to Someone With Chronic Pain

Personal Perspective: Supporting someone with chronic pain, from a psychologist who has lived it.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Social dynamics and relationships impact chronic pain symptoms—pain is more than biology.
  • Chronic pain violates social expectations that pain will end—and some words can reinforce the stigma.
  • Try "Take care of yourself" or "I'm thinking about you" or other phrases that don't assume a quick recovery.

You probably know someone who lives with chronic pain, and you’d love for them to get better as soon as possible. It’s agonizing to see a loved one suffer. If you’re the pain sufferer, you know how horrific it is to live in a body that produces non-stop pain, day after day. Holding the wish for recovery while accepting the presence of ongoing pain is a challenging task, particularly in the social, relational world.

Societal Expectations Versus the Reality of Chronic Pain

Chronic pain violates what society teaches us about pain—that it should only be acute; it should be solved somehow, at some point. It should not drag on, day after day. If it does, well—there might be something wrong with you. Yet, persistent pain is a sad reality for 1.5 billion people worldwide—1.5 billion people who are worthy of love and understanding.

I’ve taken a close look at chronic pain through lived experience, pain research, clinical practice as a psychologist, and by putting everything I’ve learned on paper in my new book, Train Your Brain to Beat Chronic Pain. Looking back, the social challenges around pain have been difficult. Well-intended comments can be paradoxically upsetting, and that small-but-significant piece of the pain experience is something I want to highlight.

Personal Story: Early Medical Trauma and the Onset of Chronic Pain

My personal journey into intermittent and then intractable pain started with a medical trauma at age 6. One night, I awoke to excruciating abdominal pain, which the pediatrician misdiagnosed as the flu. After 48 hours of agony, I went into shock and was rushed to the ER. Exploratory surgery revealed a twisted small intestine and several feet of dead tissue, which was surgically removed along with a nonviable ileocecal valve, an important sphincter muscle that keeps harmful bacteria from overgrowing. Although I was too young to understand, I nearly died. Two years later, I experienced a second blockage, emergency surgery, and hospitalization. In the wake of these procedures, I was in intermittent pain throughout childhood and adolescence.

Fast forward to my early 20s, when I became romantically involved with a fellow graduate student whom I knew deep down used alcohol a little bit too much. Yet my ego had organized itself around being the agreeable, accommodating, nice, and unproblematic person who selflessly supported others. So I didn’t really allow myself to feel upset about it. As the relationship progressed, I tried harder and harder to suppress my needs and any conscious recognition of the deeply problematic aspects of our relationship. Episodic migraines were a warning signal.

Then a day came when I experienced explosive head and shoulder pain that wouldn’t abate. For the ensuing year, I was surviving life 15 minutes at a time. My nervous system became so sensitive that I could hardly tolerate wearing a button-down shirt. Overhead light and normal noise from the television would make me uncomfortable. I was in a dangerous situation (a toxic relationship). I wasn’t listening to my emotions, and my body started to scream. The pain was so constant and so intense that I could understand—although I never had the urge—why some people with chronic pain choose to escape by suicide.1

article continues after advertisement

Despite it all, I stayed in graduate school. I saw a lot of doctors and alternative medicine specialists. I remained physically active. Through a combination of medications and supplements, chiropractic care, psychotherapy, acupuncture, meditation, functional medicine, physical therapy, and more, I started to improve. I divorced my husband and started dating the man with whom I would marry and have two beautiful children. Life was looking up, but chronic pain recovery is a long road, and I still had a ways to go.

My final year of graduate school rolled around, and I was working at a counseling center. I was surrounded by highly empathetic psychotherapists. My pain symptoms, though improving, would wax and wane. It was a social justice-oriented workplace, and I was given accommodations for my condition. If I decided I needed to, I could leave the office early. That was great, as so many others with invisible disabilities aren’t so lucky.

The Emotional Impact of “Get Well Soon” Comments on Chronic Pain Sufferers

On days that I used my accommodations, I would let colleagues know that I wasn’t feeling well and about to head out for the day. “I hope you feel better soon,” they would say. A kind statement. Yet each time I heard it, I felt kind of embarrassed and strange. Maybe a bit self-critical. My feelings didn’t make sense to me. I wondered—Why does that bother me so much?

Looking back, I see how such well-meaning words brought to the surface how much I was violating societal expectations about pain: It’s supposed to get better. My pain wasn’t acute with an end in sight. It was chronic—whether it would end for good was a complete unknown.

What to Say Instead: Supporting Someone With Chronic Pain

If you know someone who lives with chronic pain, I suggest dropping the phrase “I hope you feel better soon.” Try “Take care of yourself,” or “I’ll be thinking about you,” or “I’d love to catch up soon—text me when you’re up for a video call or a walk.” Show that you accept that their pain is ongoing, remembering that acceptance doesn’t mean giving up.

article continues after advertisement

Every chronic pain condition is unique and complex, often benefiting from a holistic, integrative, and multimodal treatment plan. Recovery is possible. Help your friends and loved ones hold grief (what they’ve lost due to pain) and hope (what they still can do and what could be) at the same time. Let them know that they’re not flawed, but rather special, incredible, and ever worthy of love.

1. If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Note: Part of this piece is an excerpt from Train Your Brain to Beat Chronic Pain, reproduced with permission from The Guilford Press.

item.title: What to Do About Screen Time This Summer
item.description:
Play

What to Do About Screen Time This Summer

6 strategies to develop a healthy play diet and reduce screen time.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • A play diet balances five core categories: social, physical, creative, free, and digital play experiences
  • To reduce screen time, identify low-cost, offline activities in your community or home projects for your kids.
  • Like a food diet, the perfect play diet balance is personalized to meet your child's age and specific needs.

Whether your child has already started their summer vacation or is just about to, you might be looking for things to keep them busy. In the best of worlds, parents don't have to work, have lots of money and resources, and live somewhere with abundant summer activities. Beaches, museums, parks, hiking trails, nearby relatives, amusement parks, camping, and many friends are close by. And your kids are excited about all these activities and very willing participants.

But what if your kids would rather spend most of their time staring at a screen, scrolling through short videos, streaming shows, diving into TikTok and Instagram, or playing video games? What should you, as a responsible parent, do about screen time this summer? After all, your kids need a break from school. The most productive way for children to learn is to play. If their preferred way of playing is on their screen, is there really anything wrong with that?

Fortunately, psychologists, pediatricians, and other childcare professionals know the answer to that question. It is yes. Non-stop screen time this summer is not healthy for your child's development, brain growth, social skills, physical fitness, or happiness. Recently, many studies have come out indicating that excessive amounts of specific types of screen time, such as social media, often lead to stress, anxiety, and depression in teenagers (Haidt, 2024). Other research has shown that too much time scrolling short videos can reduce the capacity for attention and focus (Cole et al., 2025). If this information makes you decide to eliminate screen time this summer, I wish you good luck. But if it helps you structure your summer to balance children's screen time with other activities, consider applying a well-thought-out "play diet" for your child to ensure they engage in a variety of healthy activities, including screen time, over the next few months.

One preliminary consideration in moderating your child's screen time, whether during the summer or the school year, is that it's not really about your kids being so drawn to screens. It's about how incredibly effective and engaging the technology developers have made screen time at drawing not only your kids into nonstop use, but adults as well. So don't blame your kids for wanting their screens so much. Help them understand what's happening when the screens beckon. The majority of teenagers already recognize that they're being manipulated to spend so much of their time on screens. Younger children may not have the metacognitive skills to examine their own behavior. They are far more easily influenced by parents who inform them about what they can and can't do.

5 Categories of Play

Parents, even those who are working, can insist that their kids engage in alternative activities instead of screens. A healthy and fun play diet is something most kids will readily participate in. The concept is quite simple: Children have fun and learn from many types of play. We have divided play into five different categories:

article continues after advertisement
  1. Social play: Playing and interacting with peers, siblings, parents, or teammates
  2. Physical play: Movement activities, sports, outdoor games
  3. Creative play: Imagination, pretending, art, music, exploration
  4. Free play: Play without structure, rules, or goals
  5. Digital play: Technology play involving games, screens, and media
Source: Helena Lopes / Pexels

Just like in a food diet, balance is important, but experts disagree on what that balance means. Some food nutritionists focus on a single nutrient, such as protein, while others emphasize other components, such as fiber and complex carbohydrates. They also debate the ideal proportions of healthy fats, water, and micronutrients, often depending on a person's age and health history. The same is true of a play diet. There is not one play diet that fits all kids of all ages. Your perspective, your child's specific needs, and the relative importance of the different categories of play might be more significant than just striking an equal balance across all of them.

Strategies to Develop a Healthy Play Diet

Here are six strategies to help you get started on developing a healthy play diet with your kids this summer:

  1. Discuss, do not simply impose. Consider what you, as a parent, would like to do when you go on vacation. You might want to get away from the demands of your normal life and find the ways you most readily relax. For many kids, that's to jump into their screens. Start the conversation from there.

  2. Be prepared. Make some plans for summer activities that are playful, different, and don't involve screen time.

  3. Structure screen-free times during the day. Many families find that eliminating morning screen time helps them with the rest of the day, and that allowing screen time later in the afternoon and before dinner is often the best time for kids to wind down from a physically active day.

  4. Walk the walk and model playful activities. Make an effort to engage in hobbies and activities your kids see you doing, like taking walks after dinner, planting a small garden, or playing a board game with them.

  5. Educate yourself and the kids about healthy play diets. Help them recognize how screen-based technologies capture and manipulate our attention, and help them make better decisions about how they use them.

  6. Invest in a balanced play diet this summer. If you're fortunate to have the money to engage in a variety of activities, spend it. It's worthwhile. If not, find low-cost options: community summer programs, nearby nature and hiking, visiting family or friends, getting a pet, cooking together, the local library, park and recreation programs, or starting a project at home, like an indoor or outdoor garden or a small construction project.

article continues after advertisement

A healthy play diet has many benefits, but it does not eliminate screen time. It focuses more on the positive nature of the other types of play. Swapping other activities for a child's screen time is extremely difficult. But it makes for a far richer childhood. Recognize when kids are fully engaged in a variety of other activities and celebrate it. But allow yourself some flexibility. A lengthy car trip with screen time will help keep peace in the car. Or kids’ screen time that gives parents the wherewithal to make a healthy, nutritious dinner is good for everyone. Making screen time into a family activity, like watching a movie together or sharing a favorite streaming show, can be family-building. Our argument isn't that screen time is destructive, although we do have specific concerns. It's that the absence of those other activities is what's more harmful for your kids.

item.title: Two Friendship Benefits of Perspective-Taking
item.description:
Friends

Two Friendship Benefits of Perspective-Taking

Helping children become more considerate of others and less hurt by assumptions.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Many disappointments and conflicts begin with assumptions about another person’s thoughts or intentions.
  • Perspective-taking helps children recognize how their words and actions may affect others.
  • Perspective-taking also helps children consider alternative explanations for disappointing experiences.
Source: RDNE / Pexels

With summer around the bend and the respite that comes at the end of the school year, maybe you are looking forward to a break from whatever challenges your child has been experiencing over the past few months. Or maybe you are looking at summer as an opportunity to focus on something that felt important but kept getting pushed aside. Not because it wasn’t important, but because your child’s life is busy and so is yours.

Summer Provides New Opportunities for Social Growth

Summer offers a different opportunity. With fewer academic demands and more unstructured time, children often have additional opportunities to interact with siblings, friends, and peers. Those interactions provide valuable opportunities to observe, practice, and strengthen the skills that support the development and maintenance of friendships.

Source: Kampus Production / Pexels

While there are many social skills associated with friendship, it is probably neither realistic nor necessary to focus on all of them at once. In fact, trying to tackle too many areas for improvement simultaneously is often a recipe for disappointment. Whether the goal is improving social skills, getting in shape, becoming more organized, or changing almost any behavior, meaningful change is more likely when we focus on one or two things rather than eight.

By the end of the school year, many children are tired. Day after day, all year long, they have been managing academic demands, navigating friendships, dealing with misunderstandings and conflicts, responding to expectations from teachers and parents, and trying to hold it all together. Parents are tired, too.

Source: Zaid Issac / Pexels

Focus on One Social Skill That Makes a Big Difference

The goal is not to turn summer into another school year or another list of things your child needs to work on. Instead, it is to identify one or two areas where growth might meaningfully improve your child’s social relationships. One place to start is perspective taking.

article continues after advertisement

What Is Perspective-Taking and Why Is It Important?

Many disappointments, hurt feelings, and conflicts are connected to the assumptions we make about another person’s thoughts, feelings, and intentions. This is true for adults as well as children.

We often assume we know why someone did something, what they meant by it, or how they feel about us, and then respond based on that interpretation. Sometimes we’re right. Sometimes we’re wrong. And sometimes, we simply don’t have enough information to know.

Teaching Perspective-Taking Through Everyday Conversations

As I write this, the NBA Finals are taking place. Living in New York City, it is hard to miss the excitement surrounding the Knicks. Imagine two friends talking about the series. One is enthusiastically rooting for the Knicks. The other is rooting for the Spurs. In a city full of vocal Knicks fans, the Spurs fan is already outnumbered. The Knicks fan spends several minutes talking about how terrible the Spurs are. The comments may simply reflect excitement and loyalty to a favorite team, but they may be experienced very differently by the friend standing next to them.

Perspective taking does not require us to suppress our own opinions, preferences, or enthusiasm. It involves recognizing that another person may be thinking, feeling, or experiencing the same situation differently than we are.

Source: Antonios Ferret / Pexels

Simple Questions That Help Children Build Empathy

Let’s return to our Spurs example. Imagine you overhear your child, a Knicks fan, enthusiastically telling a friend how terrible the Spurs are and that they got whipped in their own city. Depending on the situation, a parent might simply ask:

  • “Did you mean to say their team is awful, or did you mean you’re happy your team won?”
article continues after advertisement

Or perhaps later:

  • “I wonder how Tyler took that.”
  • “Did you notice Tyler’s face?”
  • “Did you notice that he got quieter?”
  • “What do you think was going through his mind?”
  • “I wonder what it was like to be the only Spurs fan in the group.”
  • “Do you think he enjoyed that conversation as much as everyone else did?”

One of the advantages of this approach is that social coaching can take less than a minute. Parents do not need to turn every social misstep into a lengthy discussion. If you make too big a deal out of it, children often tune out, experience the interaction as criticism, or become focused on what they did wrong rather than what they might do differently.

The ability to take another person’s perspective and understand their emotions is empathy. That’s what you’re cultivating when you nurture perspective-taking in your child.

Perspective-taking can also help children think differently about experiences they find disappointing.

Helping Children Handle Disappointment With Perspective-Taking

Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

Imagine your child comes home upset because they were not invited to a classmate’s birthday party. One interpretation might be, “She didn’t invite me because she doesn’t like me.” While that explanation is possible, it is only one of many possibilities.

The family may only have been able to afford a small party. Space may have been limited. Parents may have restricted the number of guests. The birthday child may have wanted to invite your child but been unable to do so. There may be family circumstances your child knows nothing about. In some cases, the issue may not involve the children at all. Two parents may not get along, and a decision made by one parent may affect a friendship between two children.

Source: Campus Production / Pexels

Helping Children Consider Alternative Explanations

The goal is not to convince your child that every disappointment has a positive explanation. Sometimes their first explanation is correct. Instead, the goal is to help them recognize that they don’t always have enough information to be sure they know why something happened or what motivated someone.

article continues after advertisement

Helping children consider alternative explanations can change how they feel and how they respond. A child who concludes, “She doesn’t like me,” is likely to feel very differently than a child who concludes, “I don’t really know why I wasn’t invited.”

Final Thoughts: Small Conversations Can Build Stronger Friendships

A brief pause. An observation. A question asked in passing.

Many disappointments, hurt feelings, and conflicts begin when we assume we know what another person was thinking, feeling, or intending. Perspective-taking encourages us to slow down long enough to consider other possibilities. Summer provides this opportunity.

item.title: The Cult of Freud
item.description:
Freudian Psychology

The Cult of Freud

What happens when a movement protects its founder instead of the truth?

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Freud built a secret inner circle to guard his theory from scrutiny and protect its “purity”.
  • In 1897, Freud reversed his findings that child sexual abuse was real, calling it fantasy, instead.
  • Freud expelled those who disagreed with him from his inner circle, forming a cult of personality.
  • Early psychoanalysis was marked by high information, thought, and emotion control.

You already speak the Freudian language. Words you use without thinking come from one man, and so does the talking cure, the foundation of nearly every psychotherapy practiced today. Many of his insights still help us, and his status as one of the “fathers of psychology” is perhaps well earned. So why would someone who has spent fifty years studying cults and undue influence look at Sigmund Freud at all?

Frankly, as someone who studies cults and treats cult survivors, I recognize cult patterns in the movement Freud built around himself. When one studies the early Freudians, what emerges is not that of an open scientific community.

It would be an improper accusation to call Freud a fraud, and I am not calling psychoanalysis a cult. However, using a metric of influence I have constructed called the Influence Continuum, which runs from healthy influence at one end to authoritarian control at the other, the early psychoanalytic movement does not sit at the healthy end.

Source: Steven Hassan / Freedom of Mind Resource Center

A Truth, Then A Reversal

In the 1800s, Freud told the medical world that the suffering of some of his patients traced back to real sexual abuse in childhood. The reception to this declaration was cold, as Vienna did not want to hear that its respectable fathers were sexually abusing their children. Eventually, Freud claimed he no longer felt confident in his theories and dropped his hypothesis that many of his patients' symptoms were caused by childhood abuse.

Some mainstream historians argue that Freud's own technique leaned on pressure and suggestion, producing the very memories it claimed to find, so he had reason to lose confidence.

Regardless, Freud would go on to write that the child's or adult child’s account of being harmed was the child's own forbidden wish, and thus the Oedipus complex grew from his own personal and professional choice to switch paradigms.

One could argue that we do not have to decide whether Freud backtracked from societal pressure or his own disillusionment. No matter how we look at it, the founder of psychoanalysis saw some reality of child sexual abuse, muddied its discovery with suggestive techniques, and then subsequently turned the field away from its reality.

The Closed Circle

Throughout the many years following Freud's earliest writings, Freud's most gifted followers began thinking for themselves, and Carl Jung, his anointed heir, was drifting toward a psychology of his own.

The solution to such perceived academic “disloyalty” came from Freud’s English disciple Ernest Jones, who suggested the creation of a secret committee to guard the founder and preserve the “purity” of the theory of psychoanalysis.

article continues after advertisement

In order to defend the cause, Freud embraced the idea and gave his blessing to a clandestine board made up of those who he deemed to be the most trustworthy and loyal to him.

Freud formalized the committee by gifting each member a golden ring. This inner circle committed to a pact of ideological loyalty, pledging never to publish research that deviated from the core principles of psychoanalytic theory without first consulting the group for approval.

The wider movement did not know it existed and the public learned of it when one member finally described it in a memoir.

The historian Phyllis Grosskurth, certainly no enemy of psychoanalysis, examined their correspondence and called the ring "a metaphor for the psychoanalytic movement itself ... a cult of personality.”

In this special circle, if you rejected some part of psychoanalytic theory, such rejection was considered proof of resistance, a symptom of your own neurosis, proof the theory was working on you. This demonstration of a thought-terminating cliche (phrases or vocabulary that end thought rather than opening it), worked as continued justification for ousting those who would disagree with the Freudians and their father. Over the years, Freud's colleagues who disagreed were treated as dissidents or heretics and excommunicated from the inner circle.

In my model of authoritarian control, which assesses a group's control over behavior, information, thought, and emotion, we can see that behavior control here limits the members’ professional activities. Information control was strict, with the founding documents sealed for decades, limited only to those who were deemed unwavering in their devotion for "pure" psychoanalysis. Thought control ran high, with a doctrine that could reframe any objection as "resistant" pathology, and emotion control was organized around a charismatic “father” and the fear of losing his regard.

Source: Steven Hassan / Freedom of Mind Resource Center

The truth the movement worked hardest to manage was the reality of child sexual abuse. Freud glimpsed it, taking his innermost circle with him, teaching clinicians to hear a survivor's account of real harm as a fantasy of desire.

The capacity to control others requires a closed system, a protected authority, and a doctrine able to absorb every objection. We must always consider what truths a movement might be purposefully reframing, even within our current practice, and within our own systems of therapy, lest we repeat the past with dogmatic adherence to the therapy of the day.

item.title: Social Media Was Never Really About Connecting With Friends
item.description:
Social Media

Social Media Was Never Really About Connecting With Friends

Tips for reducing political polarization on social media.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • Outrage drives engagement, so social media platforms amplify it by design.
  • Reordering social media feeds alone shifted partisan warmth by more than 2 points in a 2025 field study.
  • Disagreement is healthy, but contempt is what social media algorithms actually produce and reward.

When social media platforms first emerged, they were pitched as tools for connection—as a way to stay in touch with friends, share photos, and keep up with people you'd otherwise lose track of. Unfortunately, that framing was always a little optimistic. Two decades in, the evidence is clear: Social media is less about connection and more about influence (Guadagno, 2025). And nowhere is that more visible than in politics.

If you've felt like political conversations on social media seem angrier, more extreme, and more exhausting than they used to be, you're not imagining it. And it's not just because people have gotten worse. It's because the platforms are designed to make it that way.

Here's how it works. Social media algorithms are built to maximize engagement, defined as the time you spend on the platform, the posts you react to, and the content you share. It turns out that the content most likely to capture and hold your attention is content that makes you feel something strongly. Anger, outrage, and moral indignation are particularly effective. Research has found that misinformation from political elites and extreme partisan content generates higher engagement than accurate, moderate information. This is not because people are gullible, but because our cognitive systems are wired to prioritize threatening and emotionally charged signals (Weismueller, Gruner, Harrigan, Coussement, & Wang, 2024).

The consequences for real relationships are measurable. In a study my colleagues and I conducted in February 2017 (just three months after the 2016 U.S. presidential election), we surveyed 285 U.S. Facebook users about their social media experiences during the election period. Nearly a third (32.3 percent) reported unfriending someone for political reasons, and 42.8 percent reported unfollowing people for the same reasons. Participants described arguments with their connections, observed others disagreeing more, and reported losing friends and family through the unfollow and unfriend features of the platform. Most reported increased psychological distress. What makes this finding especially striking is that not one participant mentioned Russian disinformation or election interference as the cause of their interpersonal difficulties—even though these same users were the unknowing targets of a coordinated foreign influence operation (Guadagno, Olivieri, & Kimbrough, 2024).

That gap—the gap between what people experienced and their understanding of what caused it—is exactly what makes influence operations so effective. The manipulation was invisible. The damage to relationships was not.

Social Media and Affective Polarization

The result is what researchers call affective polarization: not necessarily disagreement about policy, but deepening animosity toward people on the other side. You don't just disagree with them; you find them threatening, contemptible, or incomprehensible. And social media is very good at producing that feeling, repeatedly, in your pocket, all day long.

article continues after advertisement

A 2025 study published in Science put this to a direct test. Researchers developed a browser extension that used a large language model to rerank posts in participants' X (formerly Twitter) feeds. This extension moved content expressing anti-democratic attitudes and partisan animosity lower in the feed without removing it entirely. In a preregistered 10-day field experiment with 1,256 participants conducted during the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign, reducing exposure to that content shifted how warmly participants felt toward the opposing political party by more than two points on a 100-point scale. And the effect held equally for liberals and conservatives (Piccardi, Saveski, Jia, Hancock, Tsai, & Bernstein, 2025). The study's significance isn't just in the size of the effect; it's in what it reveals about cause and effect. The platform wasn't modified. People followed the same accounts as they had prior to the study. Only the order of what they saw changed, and that was enough to move the needle on how they felt about their fellow citizens.

Resisting Polarization on Social Media

So, what can you do with this?

First, recognize that your emotional reaction to political content on social media is a product of a system optimized to produce that reaction. That doesn't mean your views aren't your own—it means they're being pushed in a particular direction by an architecture you didn't choose and can't fully see. Awareness of influence is the first step toward resisting it.

Second, seek out cross-cutting information deliberately. Research suggests that exposure to diverse political perspectives on social media can reduce perceived polarization—though the effect depends on individual factors like political interest and education (Park, 2024). The algorithm won't do this for you. You must do it yourself.

Third, notice the difference between disagreement and contempt. Disagreement is normal, necessary, and healthy in a democracy. Contempt—the feeling that the other side isn't just wrong but beneath consideration—is what polarization actually produces, and it's what makes compromise and coexistence feel impossible. If social media is consistently making you feel contempt rather than disagreement, the platform is working exactly as designed.

Social media didn't create political division. But it has become extraordinarily effective at amplifying, monetizing, and, as the 2016 election showed, weaponizing it. Understanding that mechanism is the beginning of getting some control back.

item.title: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Is a Story About People
item.description:
Resilience

Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Is a Story About People

What UAP disclosure may reveal about us.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • UAP disclosure is as much a human story as it is a scientific one.
  • People do not just receive information, they make meaning from it.
  • How we adapt may matter as much as what we discover.
Source: Sherise van Dyk / Unsplash

Much of the public conversation surrounding disclosure focuses on a single question: What are unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP)?

Are they advanced technology? Non-human intelligence? Something we have not yet imagined?

These questions are important. The mystery itself is compelling, and the search for answers is a worthy scientific endeavor. Yet there is another dimension of disclosure that often receives far less attention. Disclosure is not only a story about unidentified objects, hidden information, or unexplained phenomena. It is also a story about people.

The most profound consequences of disclosure may not emerge from what is discovered in the sky but from what happens within us when we are asked to reconsider what we believe to be true.

Throughout history, humanity has repeatedly encountered information that challenged deeply held assumptions. We learned that the Earth is not the center of the cosmos. We discovered that life evolves through natural processes. We realized that our galaxy is only one among billions. Each revelation required us to revise our understanding of reality and our place within it. History suggests that people are capable of integrating even profound revisions to their worldview, although the process is often gradual rather than immediate.(1)

How Human Psychology Processes New Revelations

The history of these discoveries is often told as a story about science. But it is equally a story about psychology. New information enters a world of existing beliefs, identities, institutions, relationships, hopes, and fears. People must make sense of it. They must decide what it means and how it fits into the narrative of their lives.

Disclosure, if it continues to unfold, will be no different.

Some individuals may experience wonder, curiosity, and excitement. Others may feel uncertainty, skepticism, anxiety, or resistance. Some may feel anger. Many will move through several of these reactions at different times. The most important question may not be whether people react but how they adapt.

Human beings are meaning-making creatures. We do not simply receive information; we interpret it. We integrate it into stories about who we are, where we came from, and what kind of future we imagine for ourselves. Whenever new information challenges those stories, a process of adjustment begins. Research suggests that restoring coherence and meaning is one of the primary ways people adapt to disruptive life events and major challenges to their assumptions.(2)

article continues after advertisement

That adjustment is evidence of one of humanity's greatest strengths.

Psychological adaptation is among the most remarkable capacities our species possesses. People survive wars, economic upheaval, natural disasters, technological revolutions, and personal tragedies. We grieve, question, learn, and eventually find ways to move forward. The human mind is not designed to avoid change. It is designed to adapt to it. Decades of resilience research suggest that adaptation, rather than lasting dysfunction, is the most common long-term outcome following significant adversity.(3)

This is why the question of disclosure extends far beyond proving or disproving the existence of non-human intelligence. Even if definitive answers emerge, the larger challenge will be helping individuals and societies integrate what those answers mean.

The public conversation often assumes that disclosure is primarily about information. In reality, it is also about trust, communication, resilience, and understanding. It is about whether institutions can communicate honestly during periods of uncertainty. It is about whether communities can discuss difficult topics without polarization and fear. It is about whether individuals can remain grounded while navigating questions that may not have immediate answers.

If disclosure confirms that humanity is not alone, it will undoubtedly be a historic scientific discovery. But it will also reveal something about us. It will show how we respond when confronted with a reality larger than the one we previously understood. It will demonstrate whether we retreat into fear and division or lean into curiosity, humility, and growth.

article continues after advertisement

What Disclosure Ultimately Reveals

In that sense, disclosure is not merely a story about what may be out there. It is a story about who we are.

The mystery of UAP may eventually be resolved. The data will accumulate. Evidence will be evaluated. Scientific conclusions will emerge. Those questions, however significant, are ultimately finite.

The human story is not.

The lasting legacy of disclosure may not be the discovery itself, but the way humanity chooses to meet it. Our capacity for adaptation, cooperation, meaning-making, and resilience may prove just as important as any revelation that emerges.

Because, in the end, disclosure is not only about understanding a larger reality.

It is about understanding ourselves.

item.title: How to Deal with Humans with Dog Problems and Vice Versa
item.description:
Relationships

How to Deal with Humans with Dog Problems and Vice Versa

A new book by Laurel Saville explains how to transform human-dog relationships.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • By learning about your canine companion you also will learn a lot about yourself if you're open to it.
  • As you learn to understand "dog" your dog will learn to understand "human"—a win-win for all.
  • Most behavioral issues we have with a dog come from our wanting them to act less like a dog.
Source: Anil Sharma/Pexels.

There can be nothing better than living with a dog (or other companion animal) and having negotiable two-way relationships in which each individual has an equal say in how they want to be treated and respected.

Of course, the tenor of these and other relationships are highly dynamic and at any given time there has to be give-and-take by each party with the goal of attaining near equality over time. But, the real-life question at hand is how can some sort of equality or near equality be achieved when humans and their dogs differ in what they want and need, sometimes from moment-to-moment, and humans and their dogs are uniquely individual? There are countless nuances to the sorts of relationships they form and how they mature.

While these on-going situations and relationships can be somewhat daunting, I was pleased to learn of a recent highly acclaimed book by award-winning writer Laurel Saville titled How to Live with a Dog: Stories and Solutions for Humans with Dog Problems and Dogs with Human Problems in which she explores the science, psychology, and emotional heart of dog-human connections with empathy and on-the-ground solutions for those people who truly want to right the wrongs of how they relate to their canine companions. As you become fluent in "dog" your dog will learn to understand "human"—a win-win for all.

MB: Why did you write How to Live with a Dog?

Laurel Saville: Around ten years ago I surprisingly and reluctantly was drawn into becoming a dog behavior consultant, turning a private passion into an unexpected profession. After a few years of this work, I began writing short pieces on social media as a way to process some of my more difficult or emotional cases and share knowledge I’d gleaned with a larger audience.

Many people who only knew me as a dog trainer read these mini-essays and asked if I’d ever thought of writing a book. I’d laugh and say, “Been there, done that.” At around the same time, I was starting to experience a lot more symptoms of Parkinson’s disease which I’d had for quite a few years by then and realized that I’d have to stop one-on-one lessons and handling dogs before too long. I started to think that a book could stand in for myself and also reach more people.

So, I started working those short pieces into longer pieces, and one thing led to another. Lots of people can tell you how to train your dog. I want to show people how very much more than mere training is possible between you and your dog.

Source: Laurel Saville.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

LS: I used to think this book would be helpful for anyone who wants to better understand and communicate, and have more fun with, their dog. I thought it would be good for people who are stuck on some dog behavior issue they can’t get past. My hope was simply to reach lots and lots of dog owners. But my readers have told me that I have a broader audience.

article continues after advertisement

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

LS: The case histories I write about reveal that the basis of most of our conflict and misunderstandings about dogs, almost every “behavioral issue” we have with a dog, comes from us humans wanting them to act less like a dog. People want dogs to stop doing all those species-specific, natural, necessary things like barking, jumping, digging, wandering. They think a leashed walk, at their pace and at their side, on a concrete sidewalk, ignoring other dogs and allowing any human to pet and poke at you is a privilege they’re bestowing on their dog.

They have no idea it’s torture for the dog. Mostly because dogs are so good natured and tolerant of us. I want people to see the fullness of what a dog is and can be in the world and in their relationship with them. I want them to want more for their dogs and their relationship with their dogs.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same?

LS: I am not a dog trainer. I know how to train dogs, for sure, and I use plenty of training techniques in my work. (Shhh, don’t tell, but I use those techniques on the humans as much as the dogs!) However, my focus is on how much more dogs and humans can have and share with each other, how much richer and nuanced their relationship can be. Humans should never settle for mere training of their dog.

MB: Are you hopeful that people embrace your suggestions the dogs and their humans will have better lives, a win-win for all?

LS: Writing a book is a labor—hard labor—of love. Most people don’t realize that only the smallest, single-digit fraction of books published make enough money to justify the work involved. So, to embark on that arduous journey as many times as I have, you have to love what you’re writing about and also the inherent difficulty of the writing process.

I also love watching people realize that something they never considered possible can blossom between them and their dogs. And then seeing their dog relax and bloom as they realize their human has finally gotten it. As I say in the book, “Isn’t it beautiful?” That moment is what I want for my clients, and now, I hope, also for my readers.

item.title: Breaking the Cycle of Abuse Requires Self-Reflection
item.description:
Shame

Breaking the Cycle of Abuse Requires Self-Reflection

Exploring personal history and emotions is the first step toward change.

Posted June 18, 2026

Key points
  • It can be extremely difficult to admit that you have been abusive to your partner and/or your children.
  • It can also feel overwhelming and even hopeless to think you can change your abusive behavior.
  • You may not be ready to begin therapy but that doesn't mean there aren't things you can do to begin to change.
  • There are action steps you can take to help you begin to change your abusive behavior.
Source: Munevver / Pexels

This is the fourth in a series about identifying and eliminating abusive behavior.

It’s not easy to face the fact that you have become abusive toward your partner and/or your children. The shame you feel when you admit this can be overwhelming. While it may feel like an impossible task to stop this behavior, it is, in fact, achievable. But it will take a conscious effort on your part, brutal honesty and patience. I am going to offer you seven steps to help you decrease or eliminate abusive behavior but because space is limited I will divide the steps into two sections: Steps 1-3 in this blog and 4-7 in a follow-up blog.

1. Identifying the Possible Roots of Your Own Behavior

It is vital that you come to understand why you have adopted the behaviors and beliefs that led you to becoming abusive. This is not to provide you with an excuse for your unacceptable behavior, but to help you understand yourself. This will, in turn, hopefully help you to come out of denial, face the truth about your childhood, stop making excuses for your behavior or blaming your partner and/or your children for the way you treat them.

There is no such thing as being born a “bad seed.” And while there are a few genetic causes for abusive or explosive behavior, this is rare. The overwhelming evidence shows that the vast majority of people who become abusive were abused and/or neglected in childhood.

Making the connection between the fact that you were either abused (verbally, emotionally, physically or sexually) or neglected as a child and the fact that you have become abusive yourself can actually be very liberating.

By doing so you will discover a way out of a very dark hole, a hole that has led you to mimic your abusive parents’ behavior, a hole that has caused you to unconsciously repeat harmful behavior. Because once you make the connection between your own abusive childhood and your current behavior you will have the opportunity to change. You don’t have to blindly follow in your parents’ footsteps.

2. Acknowledge Your Feelings of Anger, Pain, Fear and Shame

The next step is to allow yourself to acknowledge how much you have suffered because of the abuse and/or neglect you experienced. The trauma you endured caused you great pain, great fear, great pain and great shame. You need to acknowledge this to yourself, identify these feelings inside you and allow yourself to express these feelings.

article continues after advertisement

Most abused children grow up to be cut off from or numb to their feelings about being abused because it can be overwhelming to feel them. Reconnecting with your feelings can often be difficult but I guarantee that underneath the rubble of your tumultuous childhood lies intense feelings of anger, fear, pain, and shame. Ignoring your feelings, trying to put them behind you, or pretending that it wasn’t as terrible as it actually was will not help the situation.

What will help is to allow yourself to begin to express all of these feelings. Allow yourself to cry about all the pain and suffering you experienced, allow yourself to get angry about the fact that one or both of your parents took their unhappiness out on you. Allow yourself to remember the fear you felt when your abusive parent approached you with rage in their eyes, the fear you felt when they threatened to send you away, the pain and shame you felt when they told you what a disappointment you were or that they wished you had never been born.

Once you connect with these feelings it can help to write about them. For example, completing this sentence stem as many times as possible: “I’m angry at my father because_______(he always put me down, he made me feel like I was worthless)” can feel like a tremendous release. Imagining you are having a conversation with your abuser(s), telling them off and letting them know how much they hurt you can help release the emotions that have been locked in your body. Therapies like Somatic Therapy can be a very effective way to release pent-up feelings.

3. Learn how to Practice Self-compassion

Shame can be one of the most destructive emotions and is one of the most common consequences of being abused. Denying your shame simply doesn’t work. Trying to avoid being shamed again by building a defensive wall between you and others doesn’t work. Isolating yourself and avoiding others does not work. Projecting your shame onto others by abusing them the way you were abused doesn’t work. What does work is to provide yourself with compassion for your suffering. Telling yourself something like, “I’m so sorry you were treated so badly by your mother” can be enormously healing. This is called self-compassion and it is the antidote to shame.

Instead of dismissing your feelings of pain, fear and shame in order to appear strong, begin to identify and attend to your emotional wounds the way you would a physical wound. If you had a large cut on your body you wouldn’t just ignore it, hoping it would just go away. You would know that you needed to cleanse the wound and put medicine on it to help it to heal. Self-compassion can feel like a soothing balm, helping your emotional wounds to heal.

article continues after advertisement

Allowing yourself to acknowledge your suffering due to your parents’ abusive treatment of you and then comforting yourself can be the most healing actions you can take. You likely had no one to comfort you after one of your parent’s rages, you probably had no one to hold you in their arms and tell you they were sorry you felt so hurt and afraid.

Offering yourself self-compassion can feel like you are finally receiving what you needed so much as a child—validation, recognition of your suffering, comfort to help you heal. In order to learn more about this powerful strategy I highly recommend the book Self-Compassion by Kristin Neff.

I hope this blog has helped you begin your healing journey. Look for Steps 4-7 to be published soon.
